views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the Osaka G20 meeting to restart talks without firing the threatened List 4 tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese consumer goods, and without rolling back existing Section 301 tariffs or the Huawei Entity List. Condition any pause in further escalation on China returning to the pre-May draft (purchases plus enforceable IP, tech-transfer, and SOE language). Keep List 4 and export-control pressure as reserved leverage rather than using them on the eve of a leader meeting.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderately elevated, not existential and not a clean opportunity. After the May 5 breakdown and the May 10 List 3 hike to 25%, China raised duties on its ~$60B U.S. list (effective June 1), halted further soybean goodwill buying, and signaled rare-earth and "unreliable entity" counters after the May 16 Huawei Entity List. That bites a core U.S. export constituency: USDA authorized up to $16B in farm aid, soybean exports to China had already collapsed (~75% drop in 2018 value; Jan–Oct 2018 shipments down 63% y/y), and NY Fed work put the existing tariff stack at about $831 per household—costs that would jump if List 4 (phones, computers, clothing) proceeds. Markets are pricing slower growth: the 10-year yield fell from 2.69% (end-2018) to 2.05% on June 26, the 2-year to 1.77%, and the 3-month/10-year curve inverted, prompting Powell to say the Fed is "closely monitoring" trade and will "act as appropriate." That is real but still short of a +0.5 national GDP-drag reading: the expansion is intact, China’s own April IP (+5.4%) and retail sales (+7.2%) slowed, and Washington still holds unused List 4 leverage. Action should therefore be negotiate, not escalate or concede. Mnuchin said the sides were ~90% toward a text before Beijing walked back commitments and that the U.S. will re-engage if China returns to that text; a senior official said Washington will not arrive with concessions and that imposing the remaining tariffs would likely kill talks. A Buenos Aires-style pause-and-talk is the available off-ramp; a unilateral rollback would reward the May reneging, while List 4 now would hit U.S. consumers, invite full Chinese retaliation (remaining U.S. goods, rare earths, U.S. firms in China), and close the window the June 18 Trump–Xi call just opened.
key_factors: Osaka G20 Trump-Xi meeting is the first leader contact since the May collapse; best feasible outcome is a tariff truce plus resumed talks, not a signed deal
Existing $250B at 25% plus Huawei Entity List already impose costs; List 4 would shift the burden onto U.S. consumer goods and likely end negotiations
Farm-belt retaliation is the clearest U.S. vulnerability (soy halt, $16B USDA aid) and would worsen if escalation continues
Bond market and Fed reaction (10-year at 2.05%, curve inversion, Powell insurance language) show trade risk is now a macro, not just sectoral, constraint
U.S. still has unused leverage and China’s data have softened, so conceding the May text or rolling back tariffs now would give away position without a matching offer

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets negotiations going too slowly and China attempting to renegotiate; orders List 3 to 25% on May 10 and preparation of tariffs on remaining ~$300B.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (many effective June 1).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List.
Google suspends Huawei Android/GMS access; US chip suppliers pause sales; Xi visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi.
China announces it will establish an unreliable entity list targeting foreign firms that cut supplies for non-commercial reasons.
Trump and Xi agree by phone to meet at the G20 in Osaka.
U.S. 10-year yield latest 2.05% on 2019-06-26, down 0.64pp / ~24% from the lookback start.
Mnuchin: sides were about 90% toward an historic agreement before China backtracked; U.S. ready if China resumes on the pre-May texts; List 4 ~$300B consumer goods pending.
U.S. will not accept conditions on its use of tariffs and is not coming with concessions; if they go with the remaining tariffs, 'the trade talks are dead.'
NY Fed researchers: newest round of U.S. tariffs will cost the typical American household $831 annually.
USDA authorized up to $16 billion to support producers hit by retaliatory tariffs and trade disruption, including soybeans.
China put further U.S. soybean purchases on hold after the May escalation; state buyers received no new goodwill-buying orders.
Powell: Fed is closely monitoring trade developments and will act as appropriate to sustain the expansion.
China April industrial production +5.4% and retail sales +7.2% (slowest retail pace in 16 years) as the trade war intensified.
